planting.note: Set container-grown plants out in spring in the dappled shade cast by mesquite, palo verde, or ironwood canopy along a wash edge, in fast-draining sandy or rocky soil.

directions: Desert lavender is a true wash-understory specialist, naturally rooting in the filtered shade beneath taller mesquite and palo verde canopy where it escapes the most intense midday sun. Its felted, gray-green, mint-scented leaves release fragrance when brushed, and pale lavender flower spikes appear in flushes nearly year-round, drawing in bees and hummingbirds even in winter. Give it sharp drainage and withhold supplemental water once roots are established, since soggy soil is far more likely to kill it than drought. Light shaping after the main spring flush keeps the naturally sprawling habit tidier without reducing bloom.

planting.note: Nick or soak the hard seed coat before sowing, then transplant young container stock in late spring into deep, well-drained wash soil while the taproot is still small enough to tolerate disturbance.

directions: Desert ironwood is one of the great long-lived nurse trees of Sonoran Desert washes, eventually casting the dense dappled canopy that shade-loving wash understory plants depend on. Growth is extremely slow for the first several years, so plant from containers rather than attempting bare-root transplant, and expect the taproot to need an undisturbed, deeply worked planting hole. Clusters of lavender-pink, pea-like flowers appear in late spring and are followed by hard woody seedpods that persist on the tree. Young trees are notably more frost-sensitive than mature specimens and benefit from overhead frost cloth for their first few winters in cold-prone sites.

planting.note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings directly in moist sand near a wash channel, or set out container plants in spring where soil stays damp longer after storms than the surrounding desert flat.

directions: Mule fat is a fast-growing, willow-leaved pioneer shrub that colonizes the active channel and banks of desert washes wherever moisture lingers after storms, making it one of the best riparian stabilizers for restoring eroding wash edges. Cream-white flower clusters open mainly in fall and are a magnet for late-season butterflies and other pollinators when little else in the desert is blooming. It tolerates both periodic flooding and extended dry spells between storms but grows fuller and flowers more heavily with an occasional deep soak that mimics ephemeral stream flow. Cut plants back hard every few years to keep the naturally leggy habit dense and prevent it from becoming woody and sparse at the base.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in gravelly, fast-draining soil in the filtered light beneath wash-canopy trees; this mallow handles reflected afternoon shade far better than most Sonoran Desert shrubs.

directions: Superstition mallow carries soft, velvety, gray-green heart-shaped leaves that look almost silvery against the green wash canopy it naturally grows under, and it holds up well in the broken shade beneath mesquite and palo verde where many sun-loving desert shrubs sulk. Cup-shaped apricot-orange flowers open over a long season from spring through fall and draw in bees steadily. It needs very little water once established but stays fuller and blooms harder with a deep soak during the hottest summer weeks. A light shearing in late winter before new growth starts keeps the naturally loose habit from becoming rangy.

planting.note: Transplant container-grown plants into well-drained wash soil in spring, siting them in the partial shade beneath mesquite or palo verde canopy where this Sonoran coastal native naturally roots along arroyos.

directions: Baja ruellia is native to the washes and rocky arroyos of coastal Sonora and Baja California, and it thrives in the dappled shade under a mesquite bosque canopy where it keeps a tidier, more compact rounded form than it does in full sun. Clusters of lavender-purple, tubular flowers open almost continuously through frost-free months, making it a reliable nectar source when little else nearby is blooming. It is markedly drought tolerant once rooted in but rewards a monthly deep watering through the hottest stretch of summer with noticeably denser flowering. Shear lightly after a bloom flush to keep the shrub from sprawling open in the middle.

planting.note: Nick the hard seed coat and start in deep pots, then transplant small young plants into open wash margins in spring before the deep taproot is large enough to resent disturbance.

directions: Graythorn forms a dense, interlacing tangle of gray, spine-tipped stems typical of the brushy thickets that line desert wash margins across the Sonoran Desert, and it tolerates the heavy clay and caliche soils common there that reject many other natives. Small greenish-white flowers appear in spring and summer and ripen into blue-black berries that quail and other wash wildlife rely on through lean months. It needs essentially no irrigation beyond what establishes it, and its thorny, multi-stemmed habit makes it as valuable for wildlife cover and erosion control on a wash bank as for ornamental screening. Avoid overwatering mature plants, which encourages rank, floppy growth rather than the tight thicket form it holds in the wild.

planting.note: Direct sow seed into wash soil just after the first autumn rains, or set out small container plants tucked beneath larger wash shrubs where afternoon shade keeps roots cooler.

directions: American threefold is a low, rounded subshrub that is almost always found tucked into the afternoon shade cast by palo verde, mesquite, or ironwood along a wash, rarely thriving out in open full sun. Its resinous, bright green leaves and odd two-lipped yellow flower heads appear mainly from late winter into spring, giving an early nectar source before most desert wildflowers open. It establishes readily from fall-sown seed timed to seasonal rains, or from small transplants set in the same sheltered wash microclimate it favors in the wild. Cutting plants back after the spring bloom flush keeps the subshrub from going woody and sparse at the center within a few seasons.
